title: A thumb mark is not a Will

scenes.dialogue: Advocates, a Will bears a thumb impression, not a signature, at the top of every page. If the objector never pleaded that, can the Court still doubt the Will?
scenes.chip: 1 · A THUMB MARK, NOT A SIGNATURE

scenes.dialogue: The trial court granted probate, on an unregistered Will, with two attesting witnesses tied to a beneficiary's husband. So is proving the thumb mark enough?
Hi, I'm Ravishankar from LawWorld. On twenty ninth October, twenty twenty six, Honourable Justice Ramesh Chand Malviya of the Patna High Court ruled.

scenes.dialogue: An elderly, childless widow is said to have left her property to her two nieces, by a Will of December nineteen ninety four. She died a month later.
scenes.shown: An elderly, childless widow is said to have left her property to her two nieces, by a Will of December 1994. She died a month later.

scenes.dialogue: The nieces, as propounders, sought probate. Her late husband's sister objected that the Will was not genuine. After her death, her daughter carried on as the objector.
In twenty seventeen, the trial court at Begusarai granted probate. It found the thumb mark was hers, identified by the nieces' own father. The objector appealed.

scenes.dialogue: In appeal, the objector relied on the thumb mark, its position, and the missing registration. The propounders replied that these points were never pleaded at the trial.

scenes.dialogue: Finally, what did the High Court decide? Suspicions arising from the Will itself must be dispelled by the propounders, even if not pleaded in detail.
She could sign, yet the Will bears just a thumb mark, and all evidence of execution came from the beneficiaries' circle. The appeal was allowed, probate refused.
